record.summary: Australia's national AI plan, anchored in 3 goals with 3 actions each: capture the opportunity, spread the benefits and keep Australians safe. Its safety approach builds on existing, largely technology-neutral laws, with agencies and regulators keeping responsibility for AI harms in their domains, practical and risk-based protections, and targeted laws where needed. It establishes an AI Safety Institute to monitor, test and share information on emerging AI capabilities, risks and harms, and it promotes responsible practices and international engagement on AI safety.
record.notes: Released by the ministers on 2 December 2025; the Plan calls itself a starting point to be adapted as technology develops. Its 9 actions are: build smart infrastructure, back Australian AI capability, attract investment, scale AI adoption, support and train Australians, improve public services, mitigate harms, promote responsible practices and partner on global norms. Existing regulators are to report gaps in laws to the AI Safety Institute, and the government says it will intervene if more regulation is needed. Feedback on the 2024 proposals paper on mandatory guardrails informed the Plan, and the government will not proceed at this time with mandatory guardrails. The Government's response of 1 April 2026 to the Senate Select Committee on Adopting AI reports $29.8 million over 4 years from 2025-26, and $7.9 million a year from 2029-30, to establish the Institute; a committed Digital Duty of Care for technology companies; a legislative framework for automated decision-making in government services under development; and a Privacy Act requirement, from 10 December 2026, to explain substantially automated decisions in privacy policies.

verification.note: Recheck of 17 Oct 2026: stored in this run the Plan's own DISR page and the National AI Plan PDF (industry.gov.au, 2 December 2025), which now support the title, date, publisher, the 3 goals and 9 actions, the safety approach and the AI Safety Institute; official_url now points to the Plan's page. The Government response to the Senate Select Committee on Adopting AI (DISR, tabled 1 April 2026), until now the record's official_url, becomes its secondary_url and supports the funding and the related measures in the notes. A browser copy of the DISR consultation hub page on mandatory guardrails (the earlier secondary source, stored before only as a JavaScript shell) supports the decision not to proceed with mandatory guardrails. The earlier notes' MoUs with Anthropic and Microsoft are not in the stored files and were removed.

summary.quote: Keep Australians safe with legislative and regulatory frameworks that mitigate AI harms, while promoting widespread responsible practices and international engagement that upholds Australia’s values.
The plan has 3 goals: Capture the opportunity by building smart infrastructure
Agencies and regulators will retain responsibility for identifying, assessing, and addressing potential AI-related harms within their respective policy and regulatory domains.
Australia has strong existing, largely technology-neutral legal frameworks, including sector-specific guidance and standards, that can apply to AI and other emerging technologies.
Our approach focuses on harnessing the opportunities of AI while taking practical, risk-based protections that are proportionate, targeted and responsive to emerging AI risks.
A proactive approach to harms as they emerge ensures that government is continuing to update and introduce targeted laws where needed.
The AISI will monitor, test and share information on emerging AI capabilities, risks and harms.

notes.quote: The ministers launched the plan on 2 December 2025
As technology develops and confidence in AI use becomes more widespread, we will adapt and evolve the plan to capture emerging opportunities and manage new risks.

notes.locator: page 36, Building on Actions 7–9: What’s next
notes.quote: Existing regulators will continue to identify and manage harms and report any gaps in laws to the AISI.

notes.locator: page 36, Building on Actions 7–9: What’s next
notes.quote: If more regulation is needed to address bad actors or broader harms, the government will not hesitate to intervene.

The Australian Government will not proceed at this time with previous proposals to introduce mandatory guardrails for AI development and deployment. Feedback on this proposals paper informed development of the National AI Plan.
the Australian Government provided $29.8 million over 4 years from 2025–26 (and $7.9 million per year ongoing from 2029–2030) to establish the Australian AI Safety Institute.
The government has also committed to legislating a Digital Duty of Care to place the onus on technology companies to make their products safer for Australian users
AGD is developing a consistent legislative framework for the use of ADM in the delivery of government services
From 10 December 2026, the Privacy Act will require regulated entities to include information in their privacy policies about how personal information is used in substantially automated decisions
